notes:
I couldn't find something useful for every verse. A few gaps (listed at the end) are left out of the notes rather than filled from memory.

---

## Exodus 20 — Research Notes

### v. 1 — "God spoke all these words"
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik (Enduring Word) says God spoke these words aloud to all of Israel at Sinai, not just to the religious leaders. He sees the commandments as God's own moral nature put into commands, not new rules invented on the mountain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- He adds that the commandments mostly set out the law God had written on the human heart since Adam; only a few parts of the Mosaic Law are new revelation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Precept Austin points out that the Ten Commandments came straight from God, with Moses not acting as go-between. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-20-commentary
- Ellicott: Scripture calls these commandments "the Ten Words." In the Old Testament only God speaks; the New Testament mentions angels taking part. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Pulpit Commentary rejects the idea that Moses summarised Egyptian moral teaching. It notes that the second, fourth and tenth commandments were not part of Egyptian ideas of moral duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- **Modern scholarship (via Constable):** Constable says the Ten Commandments are "apodictic" law: flat commands ("You shall / shall not") that rarely appear in other ancient law codes. He also notes that, compared with codes like Hammurabi's, they are positive and short. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 2 — "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out…"
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says God reminded Israel what He had done for them before He commanded anything. Who He is and what He has done give Him the right to command. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Ellicott: The opening words make clear whose authority stands behind the commands. He adds that "God desires the obedience which springs from love, not fear." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Guzik also cites Kaiser: the opening resembles the treaties between great kings and lesser kings in the ancient Near East. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- **Do the traditions differ?** Hodge (Reformed, on ccel.org) notes that these words are an introduction, not a command. Counting the preface as a commandment forces the first and second commandments to be merged to keep the number at ten. https://ccel.org/ccel/hodge/theology3/theology3.iii.v.ii.html In the Jewish count, verse 2 is the "first word." https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=TEN COMMANDMENTS, THE

### v. 3 — "No other gods before Me"
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says this doesn't allow other gods as long as they rank behind the true God. Following Cole, he says "before Me" literally means "to My face." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Ellicott takes "before me" to mean "in addition to me." On his reading, God expects the danger to be mixing His worship with other gods, not dropping Him altogether. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Constable: This is a call to belief in one God only, not just to putting Yahweh first among many. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- **How the commandments are numbered (a real difference between churches):**
  - Reformed, Anglican and Eastern Orthodox make verse 3 the first commandment and verses 4–6 the second. Catholics and Lutherans (following Augustine) treat verses 3–6 as one commandment and split verse 17 into two. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/ten-commandments-two-tablets-the-shape-of-the-decalogue/
  - Lutheran: A Ligonier editor's note on Luther's *A Simple Way to Pray* explains that Lutherans group the first and second commandments together and find the ninth and tenth in the two bans on coveting. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/praying-the-ten-commandments-the-first-table-of-the-law
  - Hodge (Reformed): The Reformed adopted the older count used by Josephus, Philo and Origen. https://ccel.org/ccel/hodge/theology3/theology3.iii.v.ii.html
  - Constable, quoting Johnson, says the earliest count (verse 3 first, verses 4–6 second) was supported unanimously by the early church. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- **Catholic view:** Catholic Answers says Augustine's count is common to Roman Catholics and Lutherans. It denies that splitting the commandments is a Protestant move against images. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-to-split-the-ten-commandments
  - Another Catholic Answers piece says the Church is not dogmatic about the numbering, and its count follows the old Jewish grouping of "no other gods" with the ban on images. https://www.catholic.com/tract/do-catholics-worship-statues.
  - A third Catholic Answers article takes a sharper line, saying Calvin renumbered the commandments partly to strike at Catholic statues and icons. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-true-ten-commandments

### v. 4 — No idols
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says the commandment forbids not only idols of false gods but also making an image of any created thing to worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Ellicott reads verses 4–5 as one sentence: don't make an image *so as to worship it*. He notes that Moses himself approved the cherubim and the bronze serpent. In his view the commandment forbade worshipping God in a physical form. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-20.html
- Constable: The ban is on images of Yahweh, not on all pictures of creatures. Making an image would put the maker in God's place and invite worshipping the object. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- **Protestant debate (Matthew Henry, Reformed-leaning):** Henry says Rome leaves this commandment out of its popular catechisms, attaches its reason to the first commandment, and splits the tenth in two to make up the number. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_020.cfm
- **Catholic and Orthodox view:** Catholic Answers says the Eastern fathers, who honoured images even more strongly, read the commandment as forbidding only images of false gods. On this view the true God, His angels and the saints are not idols. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-to-split-the-ten-commandments
- **Modern scholarship (quoted in Constable):** Kennedy suggests that rejecting images may also have had social and economic effects. It cut off a source of wealth for priestly and royal classes and kept sacrifices circulating in the farming community. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 5 — "A jealous God, visiting the iniquity…"
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott says idolatry in the ancient world meant worshipping the images themselves, which people believed had miraculous powers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- He explains the "visiting" through natural consequences: diseases passed on, poverty inherited, the handicap of being a criminal's son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Pulpit Commentary says this kind of passed-down consequence is what is meant. Idolaters' children would start life at a disadvantage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Constable, quoting Durham: God's jealousy is part of His holiness. It falls on those who promised Him loyalty and then broke the promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- Piper (Desiring God, Baptist): The fathers' sins are punished in the children by becoming the children's own sins. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-god-visits-sins-on-the-third-and-fourth-generation He stresses the words "of those who hate me." https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/can-my-life-be-plagued-by-generational-sins-hexes-or-curses
- **Debated popular teaching ("generational curses"):**
  - GotQuestions describes a belief in "generational spirits," blamed for poverty, sickness and failure. It answers that the passage does not mention any spirits. It also says that blaming every problem today on a generational curse is unbiblical. https://www.gotquestions.org/hereditary-spirits.html
  - TGC Africa says verse 5 is among the passages most used to support such teaching. It argues the passage stresses God's justice and mercy rather than generational curses, and challenges claims common in many African churches. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-gospel-is-greater-than-your-family-history-and-parents-sins/
  - GotQuestions also notes the context is idolatry, and reads the "curse" as a punishment on the nation as a whole, not on individual families. https://www.gotquestions.org/parents-sin.html

### v. 6 — Steadfast love "to a thousand generations"
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott prefers "to the thousandth generation" (as in Deuteronomy 7:9). Sin is visited on three or four generations, but righteousness benefits descendants for ever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Pulpit: "keep my commandments" is the only way love is shown (compare John 14:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- TGC Canada notes that the NET Bible translates "a thousand generations," apparently because of the contrast with verse 5. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/detrinitate/does-god-punish-sons-for-the-sins-of-their-fathers/
- GotQuestions: "God's grace lasts a thousand times longer than His wrath." https://www.gotquestions.org/generational-curses.html

### v. 7 — The LORD's name in vain
- **Traditional reading:** Precept Austin cites Guzik's three common ways this commandment is broken: profanity, frivolity and hypocrisy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-20-commentary
- Constable: This means using God's name in a common or unworthy way. God's name stands for God Himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- Guzik notes that some Jews refuse even to write "God," in case the paper is destroyed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- **Other views:** Ellicott reports that most modern critics read it as forbidding false swearing only. He thinks Jesus' "But I say unto you" in Matthew 5:34 supports that reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm

### v. 8 — "Remember the Sabbath day"
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott notes this is the only commandment introduced with "remember." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- GotQuestions: "keep it holy" is one Hebrew word, meaning consecrate, set apart or sanctify. https://www.gotquestions.org/remember-the-Sabbath-day.html
- **Where the traditions differ:**
  - **Westminster Reformed / Puritan (Christian Sabbath):** Ligonier's guide quotes the Westminster position: one day in seven, moved from the last day to the first at Christ's resurrection, to continue to the end of the world as the Christian Sabbath. https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/the-sabbath
    - Thomas Watson (Puritan) says the substance of the commandment is keeping one day in seven, not the seventh day as such. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/watson/commandments.iv.iv.html
  - **Calvin, as read by a TGC Africa writer:** Calvin called the Sabbath a "shadow rite." He did not treat the commandment as binding, and he did not equate Sunday with the Sabbath. He kept a weekly day for public worship and the duty to give others rest. https://africa.thegospelcoalition.org/article/john-calvin-on-the-sabbath-commandment-for-christians/
  - **Baptist (Desiring God):** One writer says that under the new covenant no Christian is bound by the fourth commandment as such. Resting one day in seven is still wise. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/should-christians-keep-the-sabbath
    - Piper's older sermon says Jesus didn't abolish the Sabbath but cleared away legalism. He urges Christians to keep the day of rest on the first day of the week. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/remember-the-sabbath-day-to-keep-it-holy
  - **Wesleyan-Holiness (wesley.nnu.edu booklet):** The "Sabbath principle" (a holy day of rest after six days of work) is universal. Israel's memorial Sabbath was not meant for everyone. https://wesley.nnu.edu/fileadmin/lib/view_wc_book.php?hdm=0227 The booklet calls Sunday "the Christian memorial Sabbath", a new-covenant day remembering the resurrection.
  - **Lutheran:** Luther's Large Catechism words this commandment as "sanctify the holy-day," with "Remember the Sabbath-day" in brackets. https://www.ccel.org/l/luther/large_cat/large_catechism.html
  - **Dispensational/evangelical (Constable):** This is the only commandment not repeated for the church in the New Testament. The church has traditionally kept the first day in memory of the resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- **Catholic:** Catholic Answers words this commandment (third in its count) as "Remember to keep holy the Lord's Day." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-true-ten-commandments

### v. 9 — Six days of labour
- Guzik quotes Adam Clarke (Methodist): wasting the six days is as culpable as working on the seventh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Ellicott disagrees that six days of work is commanded. He reads the clause as a limit: don't work more than six days in seven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- The Wesleyan booklet agrees with Clarke: man is as bound to work as to rest. https://wesley.nnu.edu/fileadmin/lib/view_wc_book.php?hdm=0227

### v. 10 — No work, for the whole household
- Ellicott: The whole family shared the rest. Work was to stop, not be passed to the weaker members of the household. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Piper: You can't keep the business running through servants, animals or relatives. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/remember-the-sabbath-day-to-keep-it-holy
- Guzik: The rest reached sons, servants, strangers and even cattle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/

### v. 11 — Grounded in creation
- Ellicott suggests creation may have taken six days because one day in seven is the right share of rest for human beings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Ligonier/Westminster: The Sabbath was binding from creation, before it became the fourth commandment. https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/the-sabbath
- Watson: God not only appointed the day but blessed it. It is a day when God gives grace. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/watson/commandments.iv.iv.html

### v. 12 — Honour father and mother
- **Traditional reading:** Guzik says honouring parents is a building block of a stable society. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Constable: Parents are God's representatives to their children. This commandment underpins commandments 6–10 as the first underpins 2–4. Paul repeats it in Ephesians 6:1–3. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- On the promise of long life: Pulpit says God governs by general laws, not universal ones, so the fact that some good sons die young doesn't disprove it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- **Where the two tablets divide:** Ellicott thinks it doesn't much matter, but prefers starting the second tablet here for convenience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm Catholic Answers (following Augustine) makes this the first of seven commandments on the second tablet. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/how-to-split-the-ten-commandments

### v. 13 — No murder
- Constable: The Hebrew word means murder, not all killing. The Law itself commanded capital punishment and some wars. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- Guzik: Jesus showed the commandment also forbids hatred (Matthew 5:21–26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Pulpit thinks Jesus in Matthew 5 is extending the law on His own authority rather than just explaining it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm

### v. 14 — No adultery
- Ellicott: Adultery invades the household. The Mosaic law is unusual in treating men and women with complete equality here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Guzik: The act is condemned, but not only the act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Luther (as excerpted by Ligonier) applies it to chaste living in thought, word and deed. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/praying-the-ten-commandments-the-first-table-of-the-law

### v. 15 — No stealing
- Ellicott: The commandment protects the right to property. He notes that private property is recognised in all known states. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-20.html
- Constable takes the commandment as God's approval of private ownership in Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 16 — No false witness
- Pulpit: False witness can be public (in court) or private (slander). The wording points mainly to court testimony but doesn't exclude slander. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Guzik extends it to slander, gossip, creating false impressions, keeping silent, and even flattery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/

### v. 17 — No coveting
- **Traditional reading:** Pulpit says most ancient codes stopped at deeds, and "not one attempted to control thoughts." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: This commandment "strikes at the root". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_020.cfm
- The Biblical Illustrator calls it God's "root-extractor" and names contentment as the cure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/exodus-20.html
- Constable: A legitimate desire is different from coveting, which is obsessive desire for what isn't for sale. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- **Numbering:** Catholics split this verse into "your neighbour's wife" (9th) and "your neighbour's goods" (10th). https://www.catholic.com/tract/10-commandments The ISBE article on netbible says Catholics and Lutherans follow Exodus 20:17's order, so the 9th covers the house. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=TEN COMMANDMENTS, THE That article also argues that splitting the coveting commandment in two is fatal to the Augustinian scheme.

### v. 18 — Thunder, trumpet, smoke
- Pulpit: The combined terrors of Sinai produced a great fear. The people could not bear the manifestation of the near presence of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Ellicott: A voice that was plainly superhuman filled the people with awe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm

### v. 19 — "Speak to us yourself"
- Guzik: Afraid of dying, Israel wanted Moses as their mediator. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Constable, quoting Sailhamer: The people's fear shows a growing need for a mediator and priesthood, and prepares for the tabernacle chapters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 20 — "God has come to test you"
- Guzik: The test showed what kind of God they served, what He expected, and how weak they were. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/
- Constable, quoting Kaiser: The verse contrasts tormenting fear with healthy, trusting fear, and the healthy kind keeps us from sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- Poole's comment on Biblehub: The display of God's majesty was meant to stay before their eyes as a guard against sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/20-20.htm

### v. 21 — Moses approaches the thick darkness
- Pulpit: As the people drew back, Moses drew near; the display that drove them off attracted him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/20-21.htm
- Guzik: Moses was a forgiven murderer who came to God on the basis of grace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-20/

### v. 22 — "I have spoken to you from heaven"
- Ellicott: The opening identifies the giver of the "Book of the Covenant" (Exodus 20:22–23:33) with the one who spoke the Ten Commandments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/20.htm
- Clarke: The words were probably spoken from the upper air, which would prove there was no trickery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/exodus-20.html
- Constable, quoting Merrill: The Book of the Covenant technically begins here, and verses 22–26 introduce its specific laws. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 23 — No gods of silver or gold
- Pulpit: This partly repeats the second commandment, which shows it was especially needed. The golden calf soon proved the point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: Because of Israel's pull toward idolatry, Moses was told to press the first two commandments in particular. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_020.cfm
- Constable: The verse forbids both idols of other gods and images meant to help worship Yahweh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 24 — An altar of earth; "where I cause My name to be remembered"
- Pulpit: In the ancient world, worship everywhere included sacrifice, so altars were essential. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Constable: God allowed altars where He specially showed His presence, in addition to the central sanctuary. He cites Gideon, Samuel and Elijah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html
- Constable also cites the NET Bible note: worshippers worship where he permits, in the manner he prescribes, and with the blessings he promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 25 — No cut stones
- Pulpit: The aim was to keep altars from being carved with figures that could lead to idolatry. If no tool was used, no living creatures could be engraved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Constable: The Canaanites used cut stone for altars, so the rule probably set Israel's altars apart. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

### v. 26 — No steps
- Pulpit: The reason is decency. The rule would apply until special priestly clothing was introduced. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/exodus/20.htm
- Ellicott: Once priests' clothing prevented exposure, the rule became unnecessary, which seems to be why Solomon's altar had steps. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-20.html
- Constable: Many Canaanite altars had steps. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-20.html

---

**What I couldn't find (and left out):**
- The verse-by-verse NET Bible notes page. I only saw them quoted second-hand in Constable and TGC.
- Anything on Exodus 20 from bibleodyssey.org, oca.org or newadvent.org. The Orthodox view of images and numbering above comes only through Catholic Answers, TGC and Constable.
- A distinctly Pentecostal reading from pneumareview.com, samstorms.org or ag.org. Guzik/Enduring Word comes from the Calvary Chapel movement, but I haven't treated his notes as a "Pentecostal view."
- Anything on hyper-grace or prosperity teaching tied to this chapter, beyond the generational-curse material.
- Gill's verse comments. They appeared only as fragments in search results, so I left them out.
